card.title: Manufacture of nitric acid by Ostwald's process

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The Ostwald process is a three-temperature choreography: 800–900 °C on a Pt–Rh gauze to oxidise NH₃ to NO, a rapid quench to freeze the thermodynamically fragile NO, and cool absorption towers where 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃ with excess air circulating.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Step 2's equilibrium favours NO2 only at low temperature - the quench is chemistry, not safety.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The frozen oxide*** - NO is thermodynamically unstable at low temperature; the rapid quench freezes it long enough to be oxidised on demand in the towers.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Ostwald Process: Ammonia into Nitric Acid The Ostwald process converts ammonia into nitric acid in three steps: **catalytic oxidation of NH₃ to NO, oxidation of NO to NO₂, and absorption of NO₂ in water.** It is the industrial hinge between the Haber process (NH₃) and the entire nitrogen-chemicals industry — fertilisers, explosives, and nylon all pass through its acid.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror - **Step 1 — catalytic oxidation:** 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, over a **platinum–rhodium gauze at 800–900 °C**, with roughly 10% NH₃ in air (below the explosive limit), contact time ~10⁻³ s. - **Step 2 — oxidation of NO:** 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ — an exothermic reaction *favoured by low temperature*, so the converter's gas is **quickly cooled** (waste-heat boilers) before the oxidation towers.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Three equations, three conditions, one quench - the skeleton of every Ostwald answer.

rows.text: **NEB 2024 (3m): Describe the Ostwald process for nitric acid manufacture.** — **Step 1 — catalytic oxidation:** ammonia (about 10% in air, below the explosive limit) is passed over a **platinum–rhodium gauze at 800–900 °C** for a fraction of a second: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O.…  ·  **NEB-style (5m): The oxidation of NO to NO2 is exothermic. Explain why the Ostwald plant cools the gas rapidly after the catalytic converter, and what would happen if the gas were held hot.** — **The equilibrium:** 2NO + O₂ ⇌ 2NO₂ releases heat — low temperature favours NO₂; high temperature favours the decomposition back to NO.…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The three steps run at three different temperature regimes - hot, quenched, cool - and the quench is the design's signature.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Three steps: (1) 4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O, Pt-Rh gauze, 800-900 C, ~10% NH3 in air, millisecond contact; (2) 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2, exothermic, favoured by cold - hence rapid quench after the gauze; (3) 4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O -> 4HNO3 in absorption towers with excess air.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The Pt-Rh gauze is the plant's most valuable furniture - spent gauze is recovered for its platinum.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Each Step Has Its Own Temperature Logic - **Step 1 needs heat:** the NH₃ oxidation is run hot (800–900 °C) for rate and selectivity — the Pt–Rh gauze lights the reaction and the mixture's own oxidation sustains it; the short contact time prevents decomposition of NH₃ to N₂ (the undesired competing path).…  ·  ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Why Platinum–Rhodium, and Why a Gauze - **Catalytic demands:** NH₃ oxidation needs a catalyst active at 800–900 °C, selective for NO (not N₂), and resistant to oxidation itself — platinum is nearly unique; rhodium adds mechanical strength and reduces platinum loss (Pt vaporises slowly at operating temperature).…  ·  ### Deep dive — Ostwald: three steps, one catalyst, one absorber **Step 1** — catalytic oxidation: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, ΔH = −905 kJ, over Pt/Rh gauze at ~800–900 °C. The mixture must be lean in ammonia (≈10%) because NH₃ + O₂ can otherwise burn to N₂ — selectivity is everything.…
